title: The King of Chu and the Torn Hat Tassels
text:
King Zhuang of Chu, who ruled from 613 to 591 BC, once gave a banquet for his officers that went on into the night. According to the Han dynasty collection Shuo Yuan, compiled by Liu Xiang, a gust of wind blew out the candles. In the darkness one of the guests, drunk, tugged at the clothing of the king's favored lady.

She snatched the tassel off the man's hat and told the king. If he had the lamps relit, she said, he could find the offender by his broken hat and punish him.

The king refused. He had given the men wine, he said, and it was his own fault if they behaved badly when drunk. How could he shame a loyal officer to display a woman's virtue? Before the lights came back, he ordered every guest to tear the tassels off their hats so that all were alike. Then the party went on happily.

Some years later Chu fought the state of Jin. One officer kept charging at the front of the army, fighting with reckless courage until the enemy broke. The king asked why he had risked his life so readily. The man answered that he was the one whose tassel had been torn off that night.
lesson: Sparing someone public humiliation for a small, foolish mistake can earn their devotion for life. Shame rarely improves people; quiet mercy often does.
source: Liu Xiang, Shuo Yuan (Garden of Stories), chapter Fu En (Returning Kindness)
caveat: The story is a traditional moral anecdote and cannot be confirmed by earlier records.
